title: The Last Meal Ritual
summary: Josh and Chuck explore the history and purpose of last meals before execution, from ancient codes and Roman gladiators through Frankfurt's hangman's meal, 19th-century US public executions, and modern state practices. They cover theories on why last meals exist (humanizing the condemned, retributive ritualism), refusals as protest, Texas's 2011 end of last meals after Lawrence Russell Brewer's elaborate request and Brian Price's offer to cook, notable requests (Gary Gilmour, James Edward Smith, Ricky Ray Rector's pecan pie, Philip Workman's vegetarian pizza), practices in Japan, South Korea and China, and media responses such as Pizza Hut's 1985 commercial and Amnesty International's ad campaign. The episode closes with a listener email about a cussing dentist and a Spotify search update.
topics: Brian Price Meals to Die For

segments.title: Tour reminder
segments.summary: Hosts promote the last three live shows of the year in Orlando, Atlanta, and Nashville, with tickets via the tour link.

segments.title: Opening banter on a grim topic
segments.summary: Hosts introduce the episode, credit writer Livia, and note that last meals are a morbid, grim subject that is easy to forget is tied to executions.

segments.title: Ancient and early origins of last meals
segments.summary: Discussion of the Code of Hammurabi, early documentation of last meals among Romans, ancient Greeks and Chinese, Roman gladiators' feasts, and Aztec sacrificial feasts. Meyer's 2008 paper links the tradition to the Last Supper and Eucharist requests.

segments.title: Religion and ritualizing executions
segments.summary: Hosts discuss how more religious groups ritualize executions, using the Puritans' celebratory attitude toward death as an example.

segments.title: Frankfurt hangman's meal and getting condemned drunk
segments.summary: Frankfurt's eighteenth-century hangman's meal is described, including the 1772 meal for Susannah Margaret Brandt. Hosts also note the historical custom of getting condemned people drunk, and that modern executions do not do this.

segments.title: Last cigarettes and London ale
segments.summary: Hosts discuss the last cigarette tradition and how prisons no longer allow it. They also describe the London tradition of a last great bowl of ale at the gallows.

segments.title: US history: public executions to private ones
segments.summary: After public hangings were replaced with more private executions in the late nineteenth century, prisons began publishing details including last meal requests in newspapers. Some states later published details online; Texas stopped in the early 2000s.

segments.title: Purpose of the last meal
segments.summary: Hosts question why last meals make sense, citing a Arkansas inmate's quote comparing it to gasoline in a car with no motor.

segments.title: Theories on last meal meaning and refusals
segments.summary: Linda Ross Meyer's theory that officials and the state add meaning and reduce guilt, and Brent Cunningham's Lapham's Quarterly idea that giving a last meal restores humanity. Refusing last meals as protest is discussed, including Lawrence Hayes and a study finding innocent-claiming prisoners declined more often.

segments.title: State rules and religiosity
segments.summary: A 2010 review of state rules found spending limits in some states and denials in others. A study correlated fundamentalist Christian populations and prison spending with generous last meals, which Meyer called retributive ritualism.

segments.title: Texas ends last meals after Lawrence Russell Brewer
segments.summary: Brewer's extravagant request prompted state senator John Whitmire to object, and Texas stopped serving last meals in 2011. Brian Price, a former inmate who cooked the meals, offered to keep cooking for free and wrote the cookbook Meals to Die For.

segments.title: Status food and Price's change of heart
segments.summary: Price recounts 218 last meals cooked in ten years, common requests like cheeseburgers and fries, and how a conversation about cleaning the window stains changed his view on the death penalty. Hosts discuss status food and detour into seafood and Red Lobster.

segments.title: Symbolic last requests: Figueroa, Gilmour, Johnny Cash
segments.summary: Victor Feguer requested a single olive with a pit hoping a tree would grow from his grave. Gary Gilmour's firing squad execution in Utah and Johnny Cash's phone call singing to him are discussed.

segments.title: Voodoo dirt request and Ricky Ray Rector
segments.summary: James Edward Smith requested Rakunda dirt and was refused. Ricky Ray Rector's cognitive state and his 1992 execution are discussed, including him saving pecan pie for later.

segments.title: Notable requests: Gacy, Workman, and chain menus
segments.summary: John Wayne Gacy requested KFC and other fast food items. Hosts note many requests were Burger King and Pizza Hut. Philip Workman requested a vegetarian pizza for the homeless, and people across Tennessee ordered such pizzas on his execution day.

segments.title: Break and Georgia beer request
segments.summary: Brief break. Hosts mention a 2015 Georgia case where a man asked for a six pack of beer and was refused.

segments.title: Executions in Japan, South Korea, and China
segments.summary: Japan and South Korea are named with the US as democratic industrialized nations that still execute. In Japan, prisoners learn their execution day only on the day, and get generous meals. China's practices vary, including reports of hard boiled eggs and Saint John's blessing, a drink with the executioner.

segments.title: Timothy McVeigh and Ben and Jerry's
segments.summary: McVeigh requested Ben and Jerry's Mint chocolate chip ice cream, which hosts discuss in relation to the company's politics and whether it could refuse.

segments.title: Media response: Pizza Hut ad, Dead Man Eating, Amnesty ad
segments.summary: Pizza Hut's 1985 commercial after South Carolina's execution was pulled after backlash. The Dead Man Eating blog tracked requests, Amnesty International ran an ad with last meals of exonerated people, and Jonathan Camp Boris's book The Last Meals Project is described.

segments.title: Wrongful execution and arson junk science
segments.summary: Chuck discusses the Cameron Willingham case and a New Yorker article on arson investigation as junk science, and a Supreme Court justice's remark about clear evidence of innocent executions. Hosts mention non-executed famous last meals such as Julia Child's French onion soup.

segments.title: Listener mail: cussing dentist and Spotify update
segments.summary: A listener shares a story about a dentist who swears, and hosts joke about who it might be. Hosts give an update that a Spotify search experiment influenced search results for Barry Manilow and War Pigs.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Hosts give the email address for contacting the show and close the episode.
